subject: Calculating model likelihood for new data

messages.author: c5bc2275c2e771c3
messages.subject: Calculating model likelihood for new data
parts:
Hi Yves,

I am wondering if there is a helper function to do the following method.

I have a dataset that I split into two portions (data1 and data2). I then want to fit the model using data1 and obtain parameter estimates. Using the model estimates from data1, I'd then like to fit the same model with no free parameters to get a likelihood for data2. something like the pseudo syntax below.

data1 <- dataset[1:50,]
data2 <- dataset[51:100,]
model1 <- 'factor =~ x1 + x2 + x3'
fit1 <- cfa(model1, data1)
model2 <- fix model1 parameters ####### <- this step
fit2 <- lavaan(model2, data2)

Is this something that is easy to do and I'm just not looking at the right functions? I've tried to fix the parameter table from fit1 to have the column "free" to be 0 and so on, but the lavaan function does not return a model with a LL computed.

Thanks in advance.

-john

messages.author: af82fa98896529e2
messages.subject: Re: Calculating model likelihood for new data
parts:
This is a great idea. I made an example below. Be careful that fit indices of the validated sample are calculated from df of the model (all parameters are fixed). 

HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '

fit <- cfa(HS.model, data=HolzingerSwineford1939[HolzingerSwineford1939$school == "Pasteur",])
fitpt <- partable(fit)
fitpt$ustart[fitpt$free != 0] <- coef(fit)
fitpt$free <- 0L
fitpt$unco <- 0L

fit2 <- lavaan(fitpt, data=HolzingerSwineford1939[HolzingerSwineford1939$school == "Grant-White",], control = list(optim.method="none", optim.force.converged=TRUE))
summary(fit2)

I may make this function in semTools. Are there any papers discussed on this idea?

messages.author: 89c9fc822e34b78c
messages.subject: Re: Calculating model likelihood for new data
parts:
On 10/31/2014 03:46 PM, John Prindle wrote:
> model with no free parameters to get a likelihood for data2.

If you only need the loglikelihood, you can easily compute this 'by
hand'. Assuming multivariate normality, all we need are the
model-implied mean and covariance matrix.

For example:

library(lavaan)
HS.model <- ' visual =~ x1 + x2 + x3

textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
speed =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '

fit <- cfa(HS.model, data=HolzingerSwineford1939, meanstructure = TRUE)

Y <- fit@Data@X[[1]] # data as a matrix
Mu.hat <- fitted(fit)$mean
Sigma.hat <- fitted(fit)$cov

# loglikelihood
sum(mvtnorm:::dmvnorm(x=Y, mean=Mu.hat, sigma=Sigma.hat, log=TRUE))

# or, using the sample moments only:
n <- nobs(fit)
S <- inspect(fit, "sampstat")$cov
m <- inspect(fit, "sampstat")$mean
nvar <- length(m)

-n*nvar/2*log(2*pi) - n/2*log(det(Sigma.hat)) -
n/2*sum(diag(solve(Sigma.hat) %*% (S + tcrossprod(m-Mu.hat))))


of course, you can replace 'Y' or the sample moments 'S' and 'm' with
new data.


Yves.

realize that your original post had an fit.Rdata object attached.

Investigating this, I noticed that the problem is the (lack of)
meanstructure in your model. Therefore,

> Mu.hat
R H LC PC FS SA LP
0 0 0 0 0 0 0

but we need the means to compute the loglikelihood if we use dmvnorm. So
this gives the correct number:

> M <- inspect(fit, "sampstat")$mean
> sum(mvtnorm:::dmvnorm(x=Y, mean=M, sigma=Sigma.hat, log=TRUE))
[1] -9872.178

where we have just replaced 'Mu.hat' by 'M', the observed sample means.

Yves.

messages.author: 89c9fc822e34b78c
messages.subject: Re: Calculating model likelihood for new data
parts:
On 12/15/2015 05:06 PM, Mark Taper wrote:
> I have specified a 0 mean structure. Lavaan responds internally by
> demeaning the data (or something equivalent).

Almost. In your model syntax, no means/intercepts were explicitly
mentioned. In the single-group case, when estimator = "ML", lavaan
(0.5-20) will not add a meanstructure by default. This is usually just
fine, unless you need the model-implied means for some reason (like,
calculating the logl manually).

lavaan does not center the data; it just does model the means, and in
that case, fitted(fit)$means returns all zeroes.

You can, of course, add the means to the model. The easiest way to do
this is by adding the meanstructure = TRUE argument. Now, the 'means'
are estimated, but because we did not impose any restrictions on the
means, the model-implied means will be identical to the sample-based means.

Yves.

parts:
Now I am getting confused.  There is some communication difficulty.  

You say that lavaan (0.5-20) is not demeaning the data, but is modeling the means structure and is returning all zeros.  That statement is a little ambiguous.  It could mean a) that lavaan is fitting the mean parameters and that the fits all happen to be zero. Or, b) it could mean that lavaan is constraining the means to be zero.  Or, c) it could mean in the optimization lavaan is inserting the sample means into the likelihood function, treating them as fixed, and then reporting them as zeros.

a) is not likely because the reported parameters are identically 0.  
> all(fitted(fit)$mean==0)
[1] TRUE
This means that any estimation discrepancy from 0 is less than 10^-323.

b) doesn't seem to be the case because then the likelihood should be: 
> sum(mvtnorm:::dmvnorm(x=Y, mean=rep(0,7), sigma=Sigma.hat, log=TRUE))
[1] -9874.424
But, this  isn't what lavaan calculates.  It is instead returns:
> fitmeasures(fit,"logl")
     logl 
-9872.178 

c) May be what is going on as your calculation shows:

> M <- inspect(fit, "sampstat")$mean 
 > sum(mvtnorm:::dmvnorm(x=Y, mean=M, sigma=Sigma.hat, log=TRUE)) 
[1] -9872.178

However, because lavaan reports the fitted means as all zero, a translation of the measurement scales has occurred.  This translation is equivalent to demeaning the data as:

> y=scale(Y,center=T,scale = F)
>     sum(mvtnorm:::dmvnorm(x=y, mean=rep(0,7), sigma=Sigma.hat, log=TRUE))
[1] -9872.178


Are we on the same page?

Thanks MLT
